course.description: Java is a big platform with a small core language. This module is that core: what `==` really compares, why `int` silently wraps, how a boxed `Integer` turns a missing value into a crash, and how a `switch` became an expression that the compiler can check for you.

lessons.title: Language Core
lessons.explanation:
# 01 · Language Core

Java is a big platform with a small core language. This module is that
core: what `==` really compares, why `int` silently wraps, how a boxed
`Integer` turns a missing value into a crash, and how a `switch` became an
expression that the compiler can check for you.

None of it is exotic. All of it shows up in the first hour of any
beginner CLI project — the to-do manager, the quiz engine, the bank
simulator — and every item here is a bug someone shipped this week.

## The mental model

### 1 · Primitives hold values, everything else holds a reference

```java
int a = 1;  int b = a;  b = 99;          // a is still 1 — b got a copy

int[] xs = {1};  int[] ys = xs;  ys[0] = 99;   // xs[0] is now 99 — same array
```

The eight primitives (`int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`, `byte`,
`short`, `float`) are values. Everything else — `String`, arrays,
`Integer`, every class and record — is a reference to an object, and `==`
on references asks *"same object?"*, never *"same contents?"*.

### 2 · The operand types decide, not the variable you assign to

```java
double avg = 7 / 2;          // 3.0 — int division happened first
double ok  = (double) 7 / 2; // 3.5
long secs  = days * 86_400;  // int multiply, overflow, THEN widen
long right = days * 86_400L; // long multiply
```

### 3 · Boxing is invisible until it isn't

`int` ↔ `Integer` conversion is automatic. That is convenient right up to
the two places it bites: `==` between two `Integer`s (reference
comparison, which *happens* to work for -128..127 because of a cache), and
unboxing `null` (a `NullPointerException` on a line with no dot in it).

```java
Integer x = 1000, y = 1000;
x == y;                       // false
x.equals(y);                  // true
int n = map.get("missing");   // NullPointerException
```

### 4 · `switch` is an expression now

```java
var cmd = switch (word) {
    case "add", "a" -> Command.ADD;
    case "quit", "q" -> Command.QUIT;
    default -> Command.UNKNOWN;
};
```

Arrow arms never fall through, several labels share one arm, and the
whole thing produces a value. Switch over your own enum with *no*
`default`, and the compiler tells you when a new constant goes unhandled.

## The details that bite

1. **`==` on Strings compares objects.** Literals are interned, so tests
   with literals pass; strings read from input are not. Use `equals`, or
   `Objects.equals(a, b)` when either may be null.
2. **`int` overflow is silent.** `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` is
   `Integer.MIN_VALUE`. Use `long`, or `Math.addExact` /
   `multiplyExact` where a wrap would be a bug.
3. **`toLowerCase()` uses the default locale.** On a Turkish machine
   `"QUIT".toLowerCase()` contains a dotless `ı`. Say
   `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` for keys and commands.
4. **`Math.round` returns `long`** and rounds halves toward positive
   infinity: `Math.round(-2.5)` is `-2`.
5. **`0.0 / 0` is `NaN`, not an exception** — and `NaN` is not equal to
   anything, itself included. Guard empty inputs before you divide.
6. **Arrays are references.** A method that writes into its array
   argument changes the caller's data. Return a new array instead.
7. **`max = 0` is not "nothing seen yet".** Start from the first element,
   or from `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, or an all-negative input breaks you.

## Cheat table

| type | size | range / use | literal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int` | 32 bit | ±2.1 billion — counts, ids, indexes | `42`, `1_000` |
| `long` | 64 bit | ±9.2 quintillion — cents, millis, totals | `42L` |
| `double` | 64 bit | measurements, ratios — never money | `0.5`, `1e-9` |
| `char` | 16 bit | one UTF-16 unit; arithmetic as int | `'A'` |
| `Integer` etc. | object | nullable box; needed for generics | `Integer.valueOf(7)` |

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-count-vowels.java` | ★☆☆ | a string walk, and your first meeting with locale |
| 02 | `02-integer-division.java` | ★☆☆ | an average that keeps its fraction, a percent that doesn't overflow |
| 03 | `03-boxed-equality.java` | ★★☆ | Integer ids compared properly, and a map read that can't NPE |
| 04 | `04-command-switch.java` | ★★☆ | a to-do command parser with switch expressions |
| 05 | `05-string-equality.java` | ★☆☆ | quiz-answer checking without `==` |
| 06 | `06-overflow.java` | ★★☆ | cents that don't wrap: long, addExact, widening order |
| 07 | `07-running-totals.java` | ★☆☆ | arrays: a fresh result array, and a max that starts right |
| 08 | `08-column-names.java` | ★★★ | spreadsheet column names, base 26 with no zero |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

```
java -cp ../../_lib/out 01-count-vowels.java   # from exercises/ — yours
java -cp ../../_lib/out 01-count-vowels.java   # from solutions/ — the answer
java bootcamp/Verify.java 01                   # from the repo root — the module
```

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas`

javabootcamp/01-language-core/01-count-v.instructions:
**Concepts:** strings · loops · char  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A to-do manager wants a crude "how sayable is this tag" score, and the
proxy is the vowel count. Write countVowels: how many characters of the
text are a, e, i, o or u, in either case.

    countVowels("hello")   → 2
    countVowels("HELLO")   → 2
    countVowels("rhythm")  → 0

hint: text.charAt(i) in a counted loop, or text.chars() as a stream.
javabootcamp/01-language-core/01-count-v.explanation:
A String is not Iterable in Java, so there is no for-each over it
directly. You have three idiomatic options: a counted loop with
charAt(i), a for-each over text.toCharArray() (which copies), or
text.chars() — an IntStream of the char values — with a filter and a
count. The stream version reads like the spec, so that is what is here.
The case question has a trap. toLowerCase() with no argument uses the
DEFAULT LOCALE, and in Turkish "I".toLowerCase() is a dotless ı, not i.
Checking membership in "aeiouAEIOU" sidesteps locale entirely; when you
do need to fold case on keys, say toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).
Note that chars() yields ints, so indexOf(c) takes an int — no cast.
The classic wrong turn is "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0 without the capitals:
green on "hello", red on "HELLO".

javabootcamp/01-language-core/02-integer.instructions:
**Concepts:** int division · casts · Math.round · overflow  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A quiz engine shows each player's average score and a percentage.
Write average (the mean of the scores, fraction kept; no scores → 0.0)
and percent (part out of whole, rounded to the nearest whole percent,
halves rounding up; a whole of 0 → 0).

    average(new int[] {1, 2})          → 1.5
    average(new int[] {})              → 0.0
    percent(2, 3)                      → 67
    percent(1, 8)                      → 13     (12.5 rounds up)
    percent(30_000_000, 60_000_000)    → 50

hint: int / int is decided before any assignment sees the result.
javabootcamp/01-language-core/02-integer.explanation:
Java decides the type of an arithmetic expression from its operands,
not from where the result is going. `double avg = sum / n;` with two
ints divides as ints (1 / 2 is 0), THEN widens 0 to 0.0. The fix is to
make one operand a double before the division: `(double) sum / n`.
Casting the result — `(double) (sum / n)` — is the classic wrong turn;
it converts an already-truncated number.
percent has a second trap: `part * 100 / whole` multiplies two ints
first, and 30 million times 100 is past Integer.MAX_VALUE (about 2.1
billion), so it silently wraps negative. Writing `100.0 * part` makes
the whole expression double from the first operation.
Math.round(double) returns a long and rounds halves UP (toward positive
infinity), which is exactly "nearest, halves up" for positive numbers;
the (int) cast is safe because a percentage fits.
The empty-array case is not a detail: 0 / 0 in doubles is NaN, which
then poisons every comparison it touches. Guard it explicitly. (A
stream alternative: IntStream.of(scores).average().orElse(0.0).)

javabootcamp/01-language-core/03-boxed-e.instructions:
**Concepts:** Integer vs int · == vs equals · unboxing null · Map.getOrDefault  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A library tracker keeps member ids as Integer (they come out of maps and
may be missing). Write sameMember: true when both ids are present and
hold the same number; a missing id never matches anything, not even
another missing id. Then write loansFor: how many loans the map records
for a member, 0 when the member is not in the map.

    sameMember(7, 7)          → true
    sameMember(1000, 1000)    → true      (two separate Integer objects!)
    sameMember(null, null)    → false
    loansFor({7=2}, 7)        → 2
    loansFor({7=2}, 8)        → 0

hint: == on two Integers asks "same object?", not "same number?".
javabootcamp/01-language-core/03-boxed-e.explanation:
Integer is an object, so == compares references. It APPEARS to work in
small tests because Integer.valueOf (what autoboxing calls) caches the
values -128..127 — two boxed 7s are literally the same object. Two
boxed 1000s are not, and `a == b` is false. That is the whole trap:
code that passes every hand-written test with small ids and fails in
production the day ids pass 127.
`a.equals(b)` compares values; it needs a non-null `a`. Here the rule
also says two nulls are not a match, so the explicit null check comes
first and then equals. (Objects.equals(a, b) would say null == null is
a match, which is the wrong rule for THIS domain — read the spec.)
loansFor has the mirror-image trap: `int n = loans.get(id);` compiles,
and when the key is missing get returns null, and auto-UNBOXING null
throws NullPointerException on a line with no visible dereference.
getOrDefault(id, 0) says what you mean in one call.

javabootcamp/01-language-core/04-command.instructions:
**Concepts:** switch expressions · enums · String.split · Locale.ROOT  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A to-do manager reads commands typed at a prompt. Write parseCommand:
only the first word counts, surrounding spaces and case are ignored,
and each command has aliases. Anything else — including null or blank
input — is UNKNOWN. Then write describe, which returns the help line
shown here for each command (the enum Command is already defined):

    add | a | new          → ADD       "add a task"
    list | ls              → LIST      "list the tasks"
    done | finish | x      → DONE      "mark a task done"
    rm | remove | delete   → REMOVE    "remove a task"
    quit | exit | q        → QUIT      "leave the program"
    anything else          → UNKNOWN   "unknown command"

    parseCommand("  LS ")           → LIST
    parseCommand("add buy milk")    → ADD

hint: a switch EXPRESSION can list several labels per arm.
javabootcamp/01-language-core/04-command.explanation:
Since Java 14 `switch` can be an expression: `var c = switch (word) {
case "add", "a", "new" -> Command.ADD; ... default -> Command.UNKNOWN; };`
Arrow arms never fall through, several labels share one arm, and the
whole thing produces a value — no `break`, no forgotten assignment.
Normalise before you switch: trim, split on runs of whitespace (\\s+,
so two spaces between words do not make an empty first word), and
lowercase with Locale.ROOT. Plain toLowerCase() uses the default
locale, and on a Turkish machine "QUIT".toLowerCase() is "quıt" — the
dotless i — which matches nothing.
describe switches over the ENUM, and here the expression form earns its
keep: with no `default`, the compiler insists every constant has an arm.
Add a Command.UNDO next month and this method stops compiling until you
describe it. A `default ->` arm would silently swallow the new constant;
leave it out on purpose when you switch over your own enum.

javabootcamp/01-language-core/05-string-.instructions:
**Concepts:** String.equals · equalsIgnoreCase · Objects.equals · string pool  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A quiz engine compares a player's typed answer with the expected one.
Write isCorrect: ignore surrounding spaces and letter case; no answer
(null) is simply wrong. Then write sameText: exact, case-sensitive
content equality that is safe when either side is null.

    isCorrect("  paris ", "Paris")    → true
    isCorrect(null, "Paris")          → false
    sameText(new String("abc"), "abc") → true
    sameText(null, null)              → true

hint: == on two Strings asks whether they are the same object.
javabootcamp/01-language-core/05-string-.explanation:
`==` on objects compares references. String literals are interned
(every "abc" literal in a program is the same object), so `"abc" ==
"abc"` is true and lulls you into thinking == compares text. Any string
built at runtime — read from input, concatenated, StringBuilder'd,
`new String(...)` — is a fresh object, and == says false.
Strings compare by content with equals, and case-insensitively with
equalsIgnoreCase, which folds char by char and does NOT depend on the
default locale (unlike toLowerCase()). trim() handles the spaces.
isCorrect must check null before calling a method on `given`. Calling
`expected.equalsIgnoreCase(given)` would also be null-safe (equals on a
non-null receiver returns false for a null argument) — a common idiom
is putting the known-non-null value on the left: "yes".equals(input).
sameText is exactly Objects.equals(a, b): true if both null, false if
one is null, otherwise a.equals(b). Reach for it whenever either side
may be null.

javabootcamp/01-language-core/06-overflo.instructions:
**Concepts:** int vs long · overflow · Math.addExact · widening  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A bank simulator keeps amounts in cents. Write three helpers:
totalCents sums an array of amounts without ever overflowing; addCents
adds two int amounts but throws ArithmeticException instead of quietly
wrapping around; secondsIn converts a loan period in days to seconds.

    totalCents(new int[] {MAX, MAX})   → 4294967294L
    addCents(2, 3)                     → 5
    addCents(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1)     → ArithmeticException
    secondsIn(30_000)                  → 2592000000L

hint: in `long x = a * b;` the multiplication happens in int.
javabootcamp/01-language-core/06-overflo.explanation:
An int is 32 bits: about ±2.1 billion. Past that it does not fail, it
WRAPS — Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 is Integer.MIN_VALUE — and nothing tells
you. For money in cents, 2.1 billion cents is only $21 million.
totalCents accumulates into a long. Declaring `long sum` is enough:
`sum += amount` widens each int before adding. Summing into an int and
returning it as long is the wrong turn — the damage is already done.
addCents keeps the int type but asks the JDK to check: Math.addExact
(and multiplyExact, subtractExact, toIntExact) throw ArithmeticException
on overflow. Use them at the boundaries where a wrap would be a bug, not
a feature.
secondsIn is the subtle one. `long s = days * 86_400;` multiplies two
ints, overflows, and only THEN widens the garbage to long. Make one
operand long first: `days * 86_400L`. Same rule as int division — the
operand types decide, not the variable you assign to.

javabootcamp/01-language-core/07-running.instructions:
**Concepts:** arrays · for loops · copying · sentinels  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

An expense tracker shows spending day by day. Write runningTotal: a NEW
array where each slot is the sum of the input up to and including that
day (the input array must not change). Then write indexOfMax: the index
of the largest value, the first one if several tie, -1 for no values.

    runningTotal(new int[] {3, 1, 4})   → [3, 4, 8]
    indexOfMax(new int[] {5, 1, 5})     → 0
    indexOfMax(new int[] {-3, -1, -2})  → 1
    indexOfMax(new int[] {})            → -1

hint: what should "the biggest so far" start as, before you look?
javabootcamp/01-language-core/07-running.explanation:
Arrays have a fixed length known up front, so runningTotal allocates
`new int[daily.length]` and fills it in one pass, carrying the sum in a
local. Writing the totals back into `daily` would pass the first test
and break the caller, who still thinks they hold the per-day numbers —
mutating an argument is a side effect nobody asked for.
(Arrays.copyOf + Arrays.parallelPrefix(copy, Integer::sum) is the
library one-liner; the loop is what you should be able to write.)
indexOfMax is about the starting value. Starting `max = 0` works on
every test with a positive number in it and silently returns the wrong
index for an all-negative array. Start from the first ELEMENT instead
(index 0), after handling the empty array, and use a strict `>` so the
first of several equal maxima wins. -1 as "not found" is the same
convention as String.indexOf and List.indexOf.

javabootcamp/01-language-core/08-column-.instructions:
**Concepts:** char arithmetic · StringBuilder · base conversion · validation  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

An expense tracker exports to a spreadsheet and must name its columns
the way spreadsheets do. Write columnName (1 → "A", 26 → "Z", 27 → "AA")
and its inverse columnNumber, which is case-insensitive. Both refuse
nonsense with IllegalArgumentException: a number below 1, or a name
that is empty or contains anything but letters.

    columnName(28)        → "AB"
    columnName(702)       → "ZZ"
    columnName(703)       → "AAA"
    columnNumber("az")    → 52
    columnNumber("A1")    → IllegalArgumentException

hint: this is base 26 with no zero digit — shift by one before each %.
javabootcamp/01-language-core/08-column-.explanation:
It looks like base 26, and it nearly is: in base 26 the digits are 0-25,
but column letters run 1-26 (A=1 ... Z=26) with no zero. Plain
`n % 26` therefore maps 26 to 0 and produces "A@" or skips Z. The fix
is to subtract one BEFORE taking each digit: n--, letter = 'A' + n % 26,
n /= 26. Letters come out least-significant first, so build them in a
StringBuilder and reverse() at the end.
`(char) ('A' + k)` is char arithmetic: 'A' is the int 65, the sum is an
int, and the cast turns it back into a char. That is fine; Java chars
are UTF-16 code units and A-Z are contiguous.
columnNumber is the easy direction: Horner's rule, n = n * 26 + digit,
with digit = letter - 'A' + 1 after uppercasing. Character.toUpperCase
is locale-independent (String.toUpperCase() is not).
The round-trip test over 1..2000 is the cheapest way to catch an
off-by-one at every boundary at once — a pattern worth stealing for
any encode/decode pair you write.
